description: Hey! We’re deep into science, tech, and AI engineering, backed by a pretty solid physics and math foundation. Just looking to build something cool, jump in if that sounds like your vibe.
details:
What it does

Atlas on Fire turns NASA's active-fire detections into one consistent record from 2000 to today. That record becomes a calendar of burning activity, an early warning and a live alert service, all in one free website that works on any computer with no login.

1. The fair record (the core of the challenge).

  • MODIS (Terra since 2000, Aqua since 2002) sees fire in 1 km squares. VIIRS (Suomi NPP since 2012, NOAA-20 since 2018) sees it in 375 m squares, so it counts more fire spots for the same fire: 4.15 times more worldwide.
  • We trained a model on 2.7 million place-months that both cameras watched at the same time. It learned how to translate MODIS counts into VIIRS counts for every 1-degree square of the planet and every month.
  • Six methods competed: quantile mapping (global and regional), a simple ratio, a count regression and two LightGBM versions. They were scored on years held out from training, using a selection rule we wrote down before seeing any results. Log-target LightGBM won (error 0.357, against 0.368 to 0.586 for the others).
  • Every estimate comes with a range. The 90% ranges contain the true value 92% of the time on held-out years.
  • Months before 2012 are clearly marked as estimates in the app.

2. A 3D globe of 26 years of fire.

  • NASA Black Marble night imagery, with fire glowing on it month by month.
    • Fires by month shows where it burns;
    • Unusual shows where it burns more or less than usual for that month;
    • Fire seasons shows when each region's main fire month is.
  • A play button runs through 26 years, with an optional synthesized fire sound and the satellites' orbits.

3. A story for any place. Pick a country, a featured place, coordinates, or draw a box or shape. The panel has four tabs:

  • Now: this month against usual. It includes a tested early warning for the end of the month (in backtests it beat "assume a usual month" by 29-64% from day 14) and a next-month forecast for large areas (9% better across 127 countries in all 8 test years). Forecasts that did not pass their test were not shipped.
  • Critical period: a fire clock showing the busy months and the best months to prepare.
  • History: every year since 2001, with older-satellite estimates shown striped, plus a month-by-month calendar.
  • Advice: plain-language recommendations, each with the evidence behind it.

4. Fire Watch: a live agent.

  • Every 3 hours a GitHub Action downloads the last 2 days of NOAA-20 near-real-time detections for the whole planet. It compares each square with the usual for that place and week of the year (2018-2025).
  • It raises a warning when a square has at least 100 fire spots and at least 5 times the usual.
  • We tested this rule on California's history. It caught all 7 large disaster fires within 0-3 days, and 93% of its warnings were real large fires.

5. Ask Fire Watch: an AI assistant that cannot make up numbers.

  • Code first finds the place and gathers the facts (place story, live warnings, world trends).
  • An AI model (Llama 3.1 8B, free on Cloudflare Workers AI) then writes a short answer from those facts only.
  • A checker compares every number in the answer with the data. If one does not match, the AI tries again once. If it still fails, a fixed-rule answer is used instead.
  • The live-warning status and the safety wording are added by code, never by the AI.
  • Answers can be read aloud.

6. Insights dashboard. It shows:

  • world trends;
  • countries with rising and falling fire;
  • record fire months;
  • the northern and southern fire seasons.

Who it helps

  • Emergency responders: "Is this month already unusual here?", plus live warnings.
  • Land managers and planners: the critical fire period and the best months to prepare, for any area.
  • Scientists: a consistent 2000-2026 record without satellite jumps, with uncertainty ranges and open code.

How it works

  1. Collect: 48 yearly NASA FIRMS world archives (9.8 GB) plus the FIRMS API for 2026.
  2. Clean: the same rules for every satellite. Low-confidence detections are removed, and so are permanent heat sources such as gas flares, volcanoes and factories (only when flagged in at least 2 different years).
  3. Grid: 17,237 one-degree squares × 313 months, plus a detailed 0.25-degree grid for California.
  4. Harmonize: a pre-registered contest picks the method, and the conformal ranges are calibrated on held-out years.
  5. Publish: a GitHub Action rebuilds the site every 3 hours. The whole analysis engine was ported to TypeScript and runs in the browser. We checked that it gives the same numbers as the Python version on 8 out of 8 test areas. This lets the site run on free hosting with no server.

What we hope to achieve

We want a free, honest "fire weather report" for every place on Earth. It should say how unusual this fire season is, what usually comes next and when to prepare, built on a record people can trust because the satellite jumps are removed and every number can be checked.

Next steps:

  • add NOAA-21 and future VIIRS satellites to the same scale;
  • send live-warning notifications by email or messaging;
  • get validation help from fire agencies outside California.

Tools and technologies

  • Python:
    • DuckDB, pandas, NumPy and PyArrow for 584 million rows;
    • LightGBM, scikit-learn, statsmodels and SciPy for the models and validation;
    • Shapely for geography;
    • FastAPI for the local server.
    • GitHub Pages and GitHub Actions;
    • a Hugging Face Datasets repository for the processed data;
    • Cloudflare Workers AI for the AI assistant.
  • Local version: runs the AI on your own graphics card through Ollama (qwen2.5:7b) and can download single fire spots for any area.
  • Testing: 50 Python tests, 37 browser checks with Playwright, an engine parity check (8/8) and a speech test.

Our journey

We built Atlas on Fire in two days. Its hardest problems were satellite outages, orbit drift, a model that exploded on held-out data, and a server we could not afford. The full story is here: https://github.com/chichinadzesab-maker/atlas-on-fire/blob/main/STORY.md
